CFTC Pauses Novig, ProphetX Micro and Scorigami Contracts

Published October 23, 2026 · 4 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission has told two prediction-market exchanges, Novig and ProphetX, to hold off on listing certain sports-related contracts, warning that the self-certified products may run afoul of federal law. The move, first reported by Front Office Sports and confirmed by Legal Sports Report, is the latest sign that Washington is tightening its scrutiny of sports event contracts even as several states continue to allow similar wagers through licensed sportsbooks.

What the CFTC flagged

The CFTC sent Novig a letter warning that its "micro contracts" — markets tied to narrow, predetermined in-game events such as which team scores the first points of a basketball game — are susceptible to manipulation and should not be listed. Separately, the agency told ProphetX that its "scorigami" contracts, which pay out based on a final score that has never occurred before in a sport's history, don't meet the Commodity Exchange Act's definition of a swap. Both sets of contracts had been self-certified by the exchanges but had not yet gone live, so no trading has taken place on either product. Both companies now have the opportunity to respond to the CFTC and explain why the contracts should be allowed to list.

In a statement, the CFTC said: "Any derivatives contract offered by a CFTC-regulated exchange must be compliant with the Commodity Exchange Act. The CFTC's stay of 'micro trades' today reflect a broader commitment from Chairman Selig and the CFTC to protect consumers from potential fraud or manipulation. We will continue working with our registrants to ensure prediction markets offer the valuable information that they have for decades." ProphetX told Front Office Sports it was asked to voluntarily defer listing its scorigami contracts rather than withdraw them outright, and said it has since provided the agency additional analysis.

Why it matters

The action lands amid a broader CFTC push to tighten oversight of sports-linked prediction markets: the agency proposed a rule on Oct. 9 that would further define which event contracts count as swaps under its jurisdiction, and CFTC staff have separately raised the bar for so-called "mention markets" over manipulation concerns. It also highlights a widening gap between federal and state treatment of narrow, play-by-play "micro" bets — major leagues have pushed to restrict similar wagers in state-regulated sportsbooks over integrity concerns (the NBA already bars its sportsbook partners from offering first-basket bets, and MLB capped individual pitch bets last November following an alleged player-bettor conspiracy), while prediction-market platforms built on CFTC oversight have moved to self-certify comparable products outside that state framework. For bettors, nothing changes today — neither contract type was live — but the letters signal that federal regulators, not just state gaming boards, are now an active front in the fight over how granular a sports wager is allowed to get.
